colorants.label: Cobalt Co²⁺
colorants.why: Tetrahedral Co²⁺ absorbs in three bands across the yellow, orange and red; a fraction of a percent makes a dark blue.

colorants.label: Chromium Cr³⁺/Cr⁶⁺
colorants.why: Cr⁶⁺ takes the violet edge and Cr³⁺ a band in the orange-red; between them a green window gets through.

colorants.label: Manganese Mn³⁺
colorants.why: A broad band centered in the blue-green (about 485 nm) with a shoulder near 650 nm leaves red and some violet: rose to wine purple, the color that manganese-decolorized glass can turn.

colorants.label: Iron Fe²⁺
colorants.why: A strong absorption rising into the red and near-IR gives the blue-green edge tint of ordinary window glass.

colorants.label: Iron Fe³⁺
colorants.why: Absorbs mostly in the ultraviolet, with weak bands in the violet and two fainter ones in the green and red, which leaves a faint yellow-green. It is the same element as Fe²⁺ in a higher oxidation state; the furnace's redox sets the balance.

colorants.label: Copper Cu²⁺
colorants.why: Strong red absorption leaves turquoise, the color of copper in Egyptian faience.

colorants.label: Gold colloid
colorants.why: Surface plasmon resonance near 530 nm absorbs the green, and what is transmitted is gold-ruby red.

colorants.label: Silver colloid
colorants.why: Silver's plasmon resonance sits near 420 nm, in the violet-blue, so it transmits the yellow of silver stain.

colorants.label: CdS crystals
colorants.why: A 2.4 eV band gap absorbs everything shorter than ~515 nm, with a sharp edge, leaving a saturated yellow.

colorants.label: CdS–Se crystals
colorants.why: Replacing some sulfur with selenium narrows the gap and moves the edge toward the red, giving orange.

colorants.label: CdSe-rich crystals
colorants.why: Selenium-rich crystals move the edge to ~640 nm, giving the signal red of selenium ruby.

colorants.label: Neodymium Nd³⁺
colorants.why: Shielded 4f electrons absorb in narrow bands (green, yellow, near-IR), giving a lilac that changes with the light source.

recipes.label: Decolorize
recipes.story: Manganese absorbs in the green, where iron's tint transmits, so together they absorb a little of everything and read as gray. Glassmakers used this to decolorize. It only works for the faint tint of trace iron: a pinch of each nearly vanishes, while more of both makes the glass dark. (The real trick also involves redox chemistry this model can't show.)

recipes.label: Deep teal
recipes.story: Cobalt absorbs the orange and red; chromium absorbs the violet and red. Together they leave only a blue-green window.

recipes.label: Amber-ish
recipes.story: Ferric iron plus a touch of manganese, through a thick wall. With iron's measured bands this comes out a gray brown, not amber: Fe³⁺ takes some green and red as well as violet. Real beer-bottle amber needs the ferri-sulfide chromophore, which this model does not have.
